frames.narration: A user opens the home page. The app sends the request with the user id. The API looks up which experiment group the user is in (by a hash of the id) and starts a 200 ms budget.
Stage one is wide and cheap. The generators read the item-to-item table for the user's recent watches, ask the vector index for the nearest videos to the user's embedding, and add trending videos.

messages.label: similar to recent watches + nearest to user vector

frames.narration: The generators return 500 candidates in about 15 ms: 200 from item-to-item, 200 from the nearest-neighbour search and 100 trending. The 10 million videos have been narrowed to 500.

The ranker needs features for the user and for each video, and it reads them from the feature store's online copy in one batch. The same definitions were used to build the training data, so the numbers mean the same thing.

The model scores all 500 candidates for chance of a click and expected watch time, which takes about 40 ms. The top of the list is the best by predicted engagement, but it is eight videos from one genre.

The re-ranker removes videos the user has already watched and any that are excluded for them. It then picks 20 greedily, dividing the score of a video by one plus the number of videos of its genre already chosen, so no genre fills the page. One slot goes to a new video that has no watches yet.

The API logs one impression for each of the 20 videos shown, with its position, the model version and the experiment group. When the user watches the third video for four minutes, the app sends that too.

The nightly training job reads the log, builds new labelled examples from impressions and what followed them, retrains the ranker and refreshes the item-to-item table and the vector index. The next day's candidates come from what this user watched today, and the experiment decides whether the new model ships to everyone.
